titleEn: AI food supply chain adoption grows as buyers seek faster insights
titleZh: AI在食品供应链中的应用加速，采购方追求更快洞察
summaryZh: 本文报道了AI在食品供应链中的快速应用趋势，涵盖大型语言模型与代理式AI的区别、行业专用AI与通用AI的效果对比，以及数据质量和人工监督的重要性。文章通过FoodChain ID Scout等案例，展示了AI如何将商品追踪从人工文献审查转变为持续智能监控，并提前预警供应链风险。对智慧畜牧行业而言，其关于数据基础设施、行业专用模型和人机协作的讨论具有重要参考价值。
featuredReason: 本文系统梳理了AI在食品供应链中的落地现状与关键挑战，特别是行业专用AI与通用AI的效果差异、数据基础设施的重要性以及人机协作模式，对智慧畜牧从业者理解AI应用逻辑、避免踩坑具有直接参考价值。
contentFull:
KANSAS CITY, MO. — Artificial intelligence (AI) quickly gathers information from commodity reports, production lines and customer orders, opening up more time for buyers and purchasers.

More advanced AI programs may give recommendations, too, but successful AI implementation in supply chains will require the right program or programs, the correct data and human oversight.

AI reduces the time needed to gather information and maintain spreadsheets, said Erin Nazetta, an executive adviser for agriculture, commodities and global risk.

“It is freeing up time for buyers, purchasers and the decision-makers to focus a little bit more on relationships and decisions,” she said.

Nazetta, who has experience across investment management, banking and global agribusiness and previously worked for Rabobank and Bunge, spoke at the Sosland Purchasing Seminar, held in June in Kansas City. She electronically fielded a poll on AI in a session that had over 100 attendees. Forty-eight percent said their companies were experimenting with AI through pilots with no commitment, compared with 24% not using AI yet, 18% deployed in real workflows and 10% embedded in daily work.

“Things are moving fast,” Nazetta said. “But again, in our industry, which is still very physically driven and (where) some pieces of the information and the processes are not digitized, it’s a little bit slower than in other industries, I would say, to be able to adopt AI.”

Research from Aptean, a supplier of vertical AI and industry-specific software, showed that 23% of food and beverage organizations said that AI was essential to their workflows and decision-making, said Katherine Parr, senior food and beverage solutions consultant at Aptean.

“Daily commodity reporting is exactly the kind of activity that’s moved from a once-a-week manual pull to something people expect AI to help with every single day,” Parr said.

AI may reduce the time that lines are shut down to clean out allergens.

“You don’t want to spend all your shift time with your lines down for washouts,” Parr explained. “You want to start with the least allergenic items and then move on to the items with allergens. This can also be relevant for colors of items or flavor profiles. Having an AI tool can help intelligently schedule items in an order that helps minimize those changeovers and downtime.”

Weather and tariffs are the next frontier for AI in sourcing, she said.

“Predicting exactly how a drought affects a wheat crop, or how a new tariff schedule hits one specific imported ingredient, means layering external weather and trade data on top of operational data,” Parr said. “That’s the direction this is heading, and it’s where I expect the most value to unlock next for buyers managing ingredient risk.”

AI programs: a closer look

Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI are two examples of programs in the AI realm.

“So the way I’d put it is, a large language model is reactive,” Parr said. “You ask it something or give it a prompt, and it gives you an answer, a summary or an analysis right then. Agentic AI actually goes and does something. It can run a multi-step process on its own, like watching a vendor’s on-time performance, flagging when it slips, and routing an approval to the right person, with a human still signing off along the way.”

LLMs are fast and conversational with minimal setup, she said, but agentic AI would be better for tasks that need to happen the same way every day, such as flagging inventory nearing expiration and routing it for markdown.

“That distinction between technologies matters,” Parr said. “Our research found 63% of food and beverage organizations are using general-purpose AI, but only 46% have put in AI built specifically for their industry.

“The ones using industry-specific tools are consistently more likely to see improvements in competitive positioning, workforce morale and forecast accuracy. A general-purpose tool can answer a quick question just fine. It’s the industry-specific, workflow-aware tools that actually move the business metrics that matter.”

Aptean compared generic AI programs with industry-specific AI programs. Forecast accuracy, after switching to a generic AI program, increased by 19%, but switching to an industry-specific AI program increased accuracy by 29%.

Nazetta said industry-specific platforms might cover commodities or lengthy legal documents.

“What is it that you’re trying to solve, and what’s the best tool to get the best outcome for that task?” she said, adding, “The winners aren’t necessarily going to have the best model. The winners are going to be able to combine their proprietary data with their commercial judgment and have the ability to act on it.”

Anyone selling full automation without a human checkpoint is selling risk, said Marc Losito, vice president of regulatory solutions for FoodChain ID.

Two models in one

An LLM model answers a question, and agentic AI takes an action, said Marc Losito, vice president of regulatory solutions for FoodChain ID, which helps customers mitigate supply chain risk, strengthen audit-ready compliance and accelerate product innovation.

The company has built FoodChain ID Scout to do both. The LLM layer reads and generates language: It summarizes human-curated regulatory and commodity data or drafts a report when asked, Losito said. The agentic layer chains multiple steps together without a person prompting each one. The agentic layer pulls the data, checks it against a proprietary rule set, flags the exception and routes it to the right person.

FoodChain ID Scout connects proprietary data from FoodChain ID with partner data and public data streams such as commodity futures, weather, and geopolitical and trade feeds.

“AI does the connecting work across all of it,” Losito said. “Most solutions confirm a food safety problem after it shows up as a border rejection or a failed audit. Scout is built to catch the earlier signal — a fertilizer market shock, a crop forecast, a tariff change — and map it against the documented fraud and compliance patterns that follow, specific to a company’s own ingredient and supplier portfolio.”

AI turns commodity tracking from a manual literature review into continuous, intelligent monitoring.

“Instead of an analyst pulling CME futures, USDA WASDE data and weather feeds by hand every morning, FoodChain ID Scout ingests all of it in real time and flags deviations outside historical norms,” Losito said. “The report stops being a data dump and becomes an exception list: what moved, why and what it means downstream. Purchasing teams get the hours back and catch signals days or weeks before a manual scan would surface them.”

He gave an example of FoodChain ID Scout analysis after the Strait of Hormuz closed due to US conflicts with Iran. Since the strait carries roughly a third of global seaborne fertilizer trade, Chicago Mercantile Exchange urea futures spiked within weeks, Losito said.

“For the market, that was read as an energy story, not a food story,” he said. “But fertilizer scarcity forces farmers to cut application rates and shift acreage away from fertilizer-intensive crops, which tightens wheat, corn and soy supply, the exact inputs behind flour, starches and syrups in baked goods.”

Tightened grain supplies historically trigger economically motivated adulteration such as dilution, species substitution and mislabeled origin, he said.

“AI connects a commodity futures shift to that documented fraud pattern and gives a bakery’s sourcing team a three- to four-month head start on supplier requalification and incoming testing, instead of finding out from a border rejection,” Losito said.

Scout also is designed to watch weather anomalies against crop calendars, tariff announcements against harmonized tariff schedules and currency moves against sourcing geography.

Avoiding “garbage” data

The need for accurate data is found in a term heard often in the AI industry: garbage in, garbage out.

“So, I would say this comes back to something I tell people all the time: You don’t get to good reporting without a good data backbone first,” Parr said. “A lot of the businesses I talk to are still on QuickBooks or spreadsheets. So, before you can even think about what AI can do with commodity pricing, you need your data in one place. Once that’s true, a planner can ask a plain-language question, like which ingredient costs moved the most this week, and get an answer instead of pulling numbers out of five different systems.”

An Aptean 2026 survey found that 81% of food and beverage decision-makers said data quality and access was the biggest challenge to successfully implementing AI.

Nazetta added that data might not be perfect.

“If you have a junior analyst and still you want to go in and double-check their work, I think this is probably a similar situation,” she said.

Humans needed

After implementing AI programs, companies still need buyers, sellers and hedgers, Nazetta said. AI pulls the data together quickly, “but at the end of the day, you still need that experience and that wisdom (that) comes from within the industry and understanding what questions to ask and then ultimately being the one that pulls the trigger.”

Parr said AI can find a risk or make a recommendation, but planners or buyers can make the final call on financial decisions like purchasing commodities.

“This could look like AI making purchasing suggestions based on market conditions, vendor compliance and lead times,” she said. “Then, an experienced person can take a look, then confirm those suggestions. What we want the AI to do is take on some of the effort and time it takes to compile all those outside factors and then have a person spend time on confirmation and action.”

translationZh:
人工智能（AI）能快速从商品报告、生产线和客户订单中收集信息，为买家和采购人员腾出更多时间。

更先进的AI程序还可能给出建议，但要在供应链中成功实施AI，需要合适的程序、正确的数据以及人工监督。

农业、商品和全球风险领域的高管顾问Erin Nazetta表示，AI减少了收集信息和维护电子表格所需的时间。

“它正在为买家、采购人员和决策者腾出时间，让他们能更专注于关系和决策，”她说。

Nazetta在投资管理、银行和全球农业综合企业领域拥有丰富经验，此前曾在荷兰合作银行和邦吉公司工作。她在6月于堪萨斯城举行的Sosland采购研讨会上发表了演讲。她在一场有100多名与会者参加的会议上以电子方式就AI进行了民意调查。48%的受访者表示，他们的公司正在通过试点尝试AI，但尚未做出承诺；24%表示尚未使用AI；18%表示已部署在实际工作流程中；10%表示已嵌入日常工作。

“事情发展得很快，”Nazetta说。“但同样，在我们这个仍然非常依赖物理驱动、部分信息和流程尚未数字化的行业中，采用AI的速度会比其它行业慢一些。”

Aptean是一家垂直AI和行业专用软件的供应商。该公司高级食品饮料解决方案顾问Katherine Parr表示，Aptean的研究显示，23%的食品饮料组织表示AI对其工作流程和决策至关重要。

“每日商品报告正是那种从每周一次的人工拉取，转变为人们期望AI每天都能帮助处理的活动，”Parr说。

AI可以减少因清理过敏原而导致的停机时间。

“你不想把整个班次的时间都花在因清洗而停机上，”Parr解释道。“你想从过敏原最少的项目开始，然后再处理含过敏原的项目。这也适用于产品颜色或风味特征。拥有AI工具可以帮助智能地安排项目顺序，从而最大限度地减少这些转换和停机时间。”

她说，天气和关税是AI在采购领域的下一个前沿。

“要准确预测干旱如何影响小麦作物，或者新的关税表如何影响某一种特定进口原料，就需要将外部天气和贸易数据叠加在运营数据之上，”Parr说。“这就是发展方向，也是我认为下一步将为管理原料风险的买家解锁最大价值的领域。”

**AI程序：更深入的观察**

大型语言模型（LLM）和代理式AI是AI领域中的两个程序示例。

“所以我的说法是，大型语言模型是被动的，”Parr说。“你问它一个问题或给它一个提示，它就会立即给你一个答案、摘要或分析。代理式AI实际上会去做事情。它可以自行运行多步骤流程，比如监控供应商的准时表现，在出现下滑时标记，并将审批路由给正确的人，同时仍有人在过程中签字确认。”

她说，LLM速度快、对话式，且设置最少，但代理式AI更适合需要每天以相同方式执行的任务，例如标记临近过期的库存并将其路由进行降价处理。

“技术之间的这种区别很重要，”Parr说。“我们的研究发现，63%的食品饮料组织正在使用通用AI，但只有46%部署了专门为其行业构建的AI。”

“使用行业专用工具的企业，更有可能在竞争定位、员工士气和预测准确性方面看到改善。通用工具可以很好地回答一个快速问题。真正能推动重要业务指标的，是行业专用、工作流感知的工具。”

Aptean将通用AI程序与行业专用AI程序进行了比较。切换到通用AI程序后，预测准确性提高了19%，但切换到行业专用AI程序后，准确性提高了29%。

Nazetta表示，行业专用平台可能涵盖商品或冗长的法律文件。

“你要解决的是什么问题，什么工具能为此任务带来最佳结果？”她说，并补充道，“赢家不一定拥有最好的模型。赢家将能够把其专有数据与商业判断相结合，并有能力据此采取行动。”

FoodChain ID监管解决方案副总裁Marc Losito表示，任何销售没有人工检查点的完全自动化的人，都是在销售风险。

**两种模式合一**

FoodChain ID监管解决方案副总裁Marc Losito表示，LLM模型回答问题，而代理式AI采取行动。FoodChain ID帮助客户降低供应链风险、加强审计就绪合规性并加速产品创新。

该公司构建了FoodChain ID Scout来同时实现两者。Losito说，LLM层读取和生成语言：它总结人工策划的监管和商品数据，或在被要求时起草报告。代理层将多个步骤串联起来，无需人工逐一提示。代理层提取数据，对照专有规则集检查，标记异常并将其路由给正确的人。

FoodChain ID Scout将FoodChain ID的专有数据与合作伙伴数据以及公共数据流（如商品期货、天气、地缘政治和贸易信息）连接起来。

“AI完成了所有这些连接工作，”Losito说。“大多数解决方案是在食品安全问题以边境拒收或审计失败的形式出现后才确认问题。Scout旨在捕捉更早的信号——化肥市场冲击、作物预测、关税变化——并将其映射到随之而来的、针对公司自身原料和供应商组合的已记录欺诈和合规模式上。”

AI将商品追踪从人工文献审查转变为持续智能监控。

“分析师不再需要每天早上手动拉取CME期货、USDA WASDE数据和天气信息，FoodChain ID Scout会实时摄取所有这些数据，并标记超出历史常态的偏差，”Losito说。“报告不再是数据堆砌，而变成了异常清单：什么发生了变化、为什么变化以及它对下游意味着什么。采购团队节省了数小时，并能在人工扫描发现信号之前数天或数周就捕捉到它们。”

他举了一个例子：在美国与伊朗冲突导致霍尔木兹海峡关闭后，FoodChain ID Scout进行了分析。Losito说，由于该海峡承载着全球约三分之一的化肥海运贸易，芝加哥商品交易所尿素期货在数周内飙升。

“对市场来说，这被解读为能源故事，而不是食品故事，”他说。“但化肥短缺迫使农民减少施用量，并将种植面积从化肥密集型作物转移，这收紧了小麦、玉米和大豆的供应——正是烘焙食品中面粉、淀粉和糖浆背后的原料。”

他说，谷物供应收紧在历史上会引发经济动机的掺假行为，如稀释、物种替代和原产地标签错误。

“AI将商品期货变化与已记录的欺诈模式联系起来，让面包店的采购团队在供应商重新认证和进货检测方面提前三到四个月做好准备，而不是从边境拒收中才发现问题，”Losito说。

Scout还旨在根据作物日历监测天气异常，根据协调关税表监测关税公告，并根据采购地理监测货币变动。

**避免“垃圾”数据**

对准确数据的需求体现在AI行业中经常听到的一个术语中：垃圾进，垃圾出。

“所以，我想这又回到了我经常告诉人们的一件事：没有良好的数据骨干，就无法获得良好的报告，”Parr说。“我交谈过的许多企业仍在使用QuickBooks或电子表格。所以，在你甚至考虑AI能用商品定价做什么之前，你需要把数据集中在一个地方。一旦做到这一点，规划人员就可以用通俗语言提问，比如本周哪种原料成本变化最大，并得到答案，而不是从五个不同系统中提取数字。”

Aptean 2026年的一项调查发现，81%的食品饮料决策者表示，数据质量和访问是成功实施AI的最大挑战。

Nazetta补充说，数据可能并不完美。

“如果你有一个初级分析师，你仍然想进去复核他们的工作，我认为这可能是类似的情况，”她说。

**需要人类**

Nazetta说，在实施AI程序后，公司仍然需要买家、卖家和套期保值者。AI能快速汇总数据，“但归根结底，你仍然需要那种经验和智慧，它来自行业内部，理解该问什么问题，并最终成为扣动扳机的人。”

Parr说，AI可以发现风险或提出建议，但规划人员或买家可以对购买商品等财务决策做出最终决定。

“这可能看起来像AI根据市场条件、供应商合规性和交货时间提出采购建议，”她说。“然后，有经验的人可以查看并确认这些建议。我们希望AI做的是承担部分努力和时间来汇总所有外部因素，然后让一个人花时间确认和行动。”

Losito说，通用AI在模式检测方面很快，但在判断方面“极其糟糕”。

“它可以告诉你一个信号不寻常，”他说。“它无法确切地告诉你……”
contentHtml: Successful implementation for AI requires appropriate programs, correct data and human validation.
